intro_en: The Israel National Trail reaches its highest point here, on the summit of Mount Meron. This is one of the most beautiful segments of the trail, with spectacular lookouts from the top of the mountain. On the way to Mount Meron we pass through Bar'am Forest, home to the tallest oak trees in Israel. On the descent from the summit to Moshav Meron, we walk through open mountain scenery.
character_en: (For those walking north to south) We begin the walk with a gentle climb through Bar'am Forest, on a path that is partly open and partly among tall trees. We continue with a steady climb on a comfortable but fairly steep path that gains 300 metres of elevation up to the summit of Mount Meron. Then comes a gentle descent on a dirt road exposed to the sun, followed by a somewhat steep descent down to the Meron parking area. In total, the trail descends 600 metres of elevation.
transport_en: Har Meron Field School. Moshav Meron
pois_en: Bar'am Forest. Well-developed Mediterranean woodland, with shade, wonderful lookout points and the flowering of the "heralds of the rain". A small spring at Ein Zeved. Remains of an ancient synagogue at Horvat Shema.
important_en: The descent from Mount Meron to the Meron parking area is exposed to the sun and is not recommended in summer. For those walking from the south in the summer season, the climb on this section is exhausting.
A convenient road climbs up to the Summit parking area and allows those who find it difficult to walk only the eastern section, downhill.
The road is open even on snow days and allows an enjoyable walk on a short section only (not on the steep sections).

There is a tap at the Summit Trail parking area, but you should not rely on it always having water; it is advisable to check with hikers who have been there recently. At Horvat Hamama there is an open camping area with a water tap.
description_en:
This segment of the Israel National Trail begins on Road 899, at the point where the road crosses Nahal Dishon near Ein Aravot. The trail passes through a bridge beneath the road. Hikers starting the walk here therefore turn south along a red-marked dirt road and descend to the right into the channel of Nahal Dishon, to meet the Israel National Trail as it emerges from the bridge.
The trail follows the stream channel upstream, heading south. Water flows in this section of the stream for most of the year, and bramble bushes, willow trees and a few old mulberry trees grow alongside the channel.
The trail continues along a jeep track and crosses the channel twice. The third time the jeep track crosses the channel to the eastern bank, the Israel National Trail leaves it and continues along the western bank on a short footpath section as far as Ein Halav.
When the trail meets the jeep track again, Ein Halav can be seen above the channel.
The spring water flows in a short brook through several small pools that invite a refreshing dip. Beside the spring, within a pine grove, there is a KKL-JNF picnic area that can also serve for an overnight stop.
We continue walking on a road beside the channel and after about a kilometre we reach the Bar'am Forest Reserve. At the end of the vehicle road there is an open area surrounded by forest, partly planted and partly natural.
A blue-marked trail turns right, while the Israel National Trail continues up Nahal Dishon together with the red marking.
We advance into the "gloom of the forest", in among the trees of Bar'am Forest, one of the most beautiful tracts of natural woodland to be found in Israel.
Beside the trail we see mainly Palestine oak (common oak) trees, but also Mount Tabor oaks, the oak species that sheds its leaves in winter and prefers to grow at altitude. Besides the two oak species, Bar'am Forest is home to further tree species: bay laurel, Palestine terebinth (pistacia), Syrian maple and storax, as well as climbers such as spiny smilax and wild asparagus. It is worth keeping your ears open for the calls of birds and other animals in the depths of the woodland.
Menahem Zaharoni, a nature teacher who was among the founders of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, wrote of the magic and special feelings of the woodland: "Once, at the dawn of creative man's existence, the woodland covered the entire mountainous part of our country. Man cleared the forest and prepared its soil for agricultural cultivation: 'Get thee up to the forest, and cut down for thyself there' (Joshua 17:15), Joshua advises the children of Joseph, who claim that their inheritance is not enough to live on since they are 'a great people'. Yet even after thousands of years of destruction, wonderful corners of forest remain in our country. Modern man finds in the woodland a release from the stresses of his life, clear air, rest and tranquillity, and aesthetic pleasure too. We are commanded to protect nature as a whole and the woodland in particular."
We pass the confluence of Nahal Dishon and Nahal Tzivon, and the Israel National Trail continues along the right-hand channel into Nahal Tzivon. After walking another 2.5 km or so, we reach a bend of Road 89 within the channel of Nahal Tzivon. On the other side of the road, the trail continues along the channel of Nahal Tzivon through low woodland.
Beside the trail grow thorny broom bushes (Calicotome), a plant with green stems that flowers in spring; its yellow pea-like flowers give off a pleasant scent that attracts large carpenter bees, which pollinate it.
The Israel National Trail arrives at the overnight campsite at Horvat Hamama, beside the road that climbs to Mount Meron. There is a water tap at the campsite.
From the overnight campsite, the Israel National Trail climbs to the summit of Mount Meron, together with the black marking.
At Horvat Hamama the elevation is about 900 metres above sea level, and at the end of the climb, on the summit of Mount Meron, the elevation is about 1,200 metres. But the trail to the summit is not steep and most of it is accompanied by the shade of the woodland.
After a short walk, we pass Ein Hamama, a small layer spring.
The way to the summit runs along the national watershed line. The channels to the west are tributaries of Nahal Keziv, which flows to the Mediterranean Sea, while the mountain slopes east of the trail drain into Nahal Dishon and its tributaries, which the Israel National Trail also follows. At the end of its course, Nahal Dishon empties into the Jordan River in the Hula Valley.
Along the way, among the woodland trees, we can pick out the strawberry tree (arbutus), notable for its red trunk and branches, and the Judas tree, a deciduous tree that blooms pink in spring and has large heart-shaped leaves.
When the trail reaches the crest of the Mount Neria ridge, a fine view opens to the north over the Dalton Plateau, Gush Halav, Sasa, Dovev and Bar'am. From the lookout, villages across the border in Lebanon can also be seen. You can notice the difference between the Israeli terrain and the distant terrain across the border in Lebanon, which is bare and brownish-yellow in colour.
The Mount Meron massif is one of the largest and oldest nature reserves in Israel. The mountain stands out for its green colour all year round. Here we can feel at close hand the importance of nature conservation and its effect on the environment in which we live and hike. Thanks to it, the Israel National Trail passes through well-developed woodland, and the dominant colour around us is green.
After a short walk from the lookout, the Israel National Trail joins the "Summit Trail", which circles the summit of Mount Meron with red marking. The Israel National Trail circles the summit clockwise, and at the junction with the red trail we turn left.
The summit of Mount Meron (1,204 metres above sea level) is the highest point in Israel west of the Jordan. Precipitation is abundant (an average of about 900 mm a year, with several days of snow) and average temperatures are low.
Several rare plants grow on the summit for which this is almost their only habitat in Israel. Among them are the Greek cyclamen and the Meron orchid (Orchis galilaea), an orchid species first found on Mount Meron, hence its Hebrew name. Also growing on the mountain are the rare Galilee garlic (Allium) and the woodland peony. In autumn, several "heralds of autumn" can be seen beside the trail, such as sternbergias, crocuses and colchicums.
Along the Summit Trail, several lookouts open to the north and east towards Mount Hermon and the Golan Heights. We can look out over the Dalton Plateau, with Dalton Lake prominent at its centre, Mount Canaan, Safed and southern Lebanon.
On completing the circuit of the summit of Mount Meron, the Israel National Trail reaches the Summit parking area. This is a recommended place to fill up with water and take a break at the tables in the shade of the trees surrounding the parking area.
The Israel National Trail continues from the south-western corner of the parking area heading south, together with the blue marking. After a short walk, we leave the woodland and reach a dirt road. The Israel National Trail turns right onto the road, westward towards Har Ofa'im.
After skirting orchard plots to the north, we turn south, with the large Druze village of Beit Jann visible ahead.
Beside a large tree, the blue trail turns west, while the Israel National Trail turns east to Khirbet Bak, a site of Jewish settlement from the 19th century. Rabbi Israel Bak, owner of a printing house in Safed, received land on the top of Mount Meron from Ibrahim Pasha, the Egyptian governor of the country in those years, and established a small village there. After an earthquake severely damaged the city of Safed in 1837, the Bak family, together with several other Safed families, moved to live at the site.
In 1839 the philanthropist Moses Montefiore and his wife Judith visited the site. Judith recorded her impressions of the visit in her diary: "We rode until we reached the village, which comprised 6 houses, with a barn and stables. A very small settlement, and yet cultivated and well kept... A man came towards us and called out to us in the holy tongue: 'Welcome'." A short time later the settlement was abandoned because of a war that broke out between Ibrahim Pasha and the Turkish Sultan. The remains of the Bak family's village that we see on the ground: a well, a spring, terraces and a few old trees.
The Israel National Trail continues east, passes through woodland and reaches a green-marked dirt road. We continue a short distance with the green marking, and when we reach a road junction we turn left. We pass a memorial erected by the Tafesh family of Beit Jann in memory of the 44 victims of the Carmel fire disaster, one of whom was a member of the family, Adal.
A short distance after the memorial, the trail turns south and reaches a small grove with another memorial at its centre, to the soldier Salah Tafesh, who was killed in battle in Lebanon in 1992. Beside the road there is also a seasonal winter pool.
The Israel National Trail turns east, to the start of the descent to Meron. Here, at an elevation of about 1,000 metres above sea level, Nahal Meron begins; it is a tributary of Nahal Amud, which flows from here for about 25 km and empties into the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), 212 metres below sea level.
After a short walk on a dirt road, we turn left and enter the woodland. On the way to Ein Zeved, we see to the left of the trail a fence around the mouth of a pit. This is a hutta, a deep chimney-shaped shaft formed by a natural process of karstic dissolution. It is one of many dozens of such shafts found on the Mount Meron ridge.
Ein Zeved lies in a large clearing, at the centre of which stands a large three-armed oak tree inviting us to rest in its shade; beneath the tree the spring emerges within a stone-lined pit.
Down the mountain, we also pass "Elijah's Chair", a natural stone pillar on which, according to legend, the prophet Elijah will sit at the End of Days.
Further along the way, on the trail, there is a unique and impressive burial structure built of large stones. According to tradition, Shammai the Elder is buried here; he was the counterpart of Hillel the Elder in leading the Sanhedrin court ("the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel"). Beside the burial structure, to the east further along the ridge, the remains of an ancient synagogue were found at Horvat Shema. After the destruction of the Second Temple and after the Bar Kokhba revolt, the centre of Jewish life in the country moved to the Galilee. In that period the synagogue developed as the Jewish religious institution replacing the Temple, a place for gathering, prayer and Torah study. Over the years, the remains of many Jewish settlements have been uncovered in the Galilee and the Golan, including synagogues from the first centuries CE.
To the left of the road, on the opposite mountain ridge at the edge of Moshav Meron, we can see the compound of the tomb of the Rashbi, Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai, the site to which crowds of celebrants ascend on Lag BaOmer to take part in the hillula festivities. Part of the road descending to Nahal Meron runs parallel to the channel of Nahal Sod ("Secret Stream"). The stream's name alludes to the Rashbi, a Tannaitic sage who lived and worked in the 2nd century CE. Tradition attributes to the Rashbi the writing of the Zohar, a central book of Kabbalah and Jewish mysticism.
In the channel of Nahal Meron we walk on a paved road as far as the "Pitul (Hairpin) parking area", the end point of the segment.
Further recommendations in the area
A tour, and many restaurants and food shops, in the village of Jish (Gush Halav).
Lookouts, vegetarian restaurants and shops in Amirim.
A boutique winery in the small community of Or HaGanuz. Not on Shabbat.
lodging_en: Camping at the Har Meron Field School
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
